mappings.note: The device sailors used when stars were hidden -- a magnetic compass. LO-36 names using a compass to find directions.
Naturally occurring magnets are lodestones. Identifying a material by name, LO-27.
Name a common artificial magnet shape. Identification by appearance, LO-27.
Materials attracted to a magnet are magnetic materials. Naming a class by observable property, LO-29.
Give a magnetic material other than iron. Placing nickel or cobalt in the magnetic class, LO-29.
Materials not attracted are non-magnetic. The complementary class, LO-29.
Where the filings gather on a bar magnet. Recall of the activity's observed result, LO-30.
The ends of a magnet are its poles. Naming a part from an observable feature, LO-27.
A magnet has two poles. Identification of the structure, LO-27.
Whether a single pole can exist alone. Explaining why poles are always paired, LO-32.
The direction a freely suspended magnet settles in. LO-30's own worked example.
The north-pointing end is the North-seeking pole. Naming a pole from its behaviour, LO-27.
WHY the suspended magnet aligns north-south -- Earth behaves like a giant magnet. The cause is what is marked, LO-31.
The compass magnet is needle-shaped. Identification by appearance, LO-27.
The matsya-yantra named. An applied navigational device, LO-36.
North near South attracts. The pole-interaction phenomenon, LO-32.
North near North repels. The other half of the same phenomenon, LO-32.
Whether the magnetic effect passes through wood. Explaining that the force acts through non-magnetic material, LO-32.
One way careless handling destroys magnetism. Practical care of equipment, LO-36.
How to store bar magnets in pairs with wood and keepers. A practical handling rule, LO-36.
Differentiate natural from artificial magnets with an example. The verb is 'differentiate', on the basis of origin, LO-28.
List three common magnet shapes. Identification by appearance, LO-27.
What magnetic materials are, with two examples. Defining and populating a class, LO-29.
What non-magnetic materials are, with daily-life examples. The complementary class, LO-29.
Describe what the iron-filings activity shows and what it indicates. Reporting and interpreting a conducted investigation, LO-30.
Names the two poles and says what breaking the magnet does. Explaining the pole phenomena, LO-32.
Why a suspended bar magnet always points one way. The Earth's magnetism as the cause, LO-31.
How the north-south alignment is put to work in a compass. Application to direction-finding, LO-36's own example.
Describe how a simple compass is built -- pivoted needle, transparent cover, marked dial. Construction of a device and how it works, LO-35.
Magnetise a sewing needle by stroking it 30 to 40 times in one direction. The making step of the homemade compass, LO-35.
What the matsya-yantra was and how it found directions at sea. Applied navigation, LO-36.
State the rule of attraction and repulsion. The governing phenomenon, LO-32.
Use repulsion to tell a magnet from mere iron. A differentiation of two materials by which behaviours each can show, LO-28.
What the compass needle does when a magnet's North pole approaches its North pole. Predicting from the repulsion rule, LO-32.
What the wood, cardboard and plastic investigation concluded. The conclusion of a conducted investigation, LO-30; the phenomenon itself was mapped to LO-32 where the item asked for it directly.
How poles are marked when not labelled -- a white dot, red or blue paint. Identification by appearance, LO-27.
Two precautions to keep magnets from weakening. Practical care in everyday use, LO-36.
How to store two bar magnets safely. The same practical register, LO-36.
Why a lone pole cannot exist, even in the smallest fragment. Explaining the phenomenon, LO-32.
Star navigation, its failure in storms, and how the compass solved it. An applied problem solved by the chapter's learning, LO-36.
Difference between magnetic and non-magnetic materials (LO-28) AND how to test a given material with a bar magnet (LO-30). Both halves are explicitly asked.
Define poles, then describe the iron-filings experiment and the distribution observed. The experiment is the bulk of the item, LO-30.
The directive property, how it finds directions, and why plain iron lacks it. The 'why not iron' clause makes the cause the marked part, LO-31.
Full build of a compass from needle, cork, magnet and water. LO-35's construct-a-model-from-surrounding-materials outcome.
Attraction and repulsion explained (LO-32), plus why repulsion is the surer test -- because iron can only be attracted (LO-28, differentiating magnet from magnetic material).
Identify the magnet among two identical bars using nothing else, by free suspension. Designing and running the investigation, LO-30.
Locate the poles of an unmarked magnet using Earth's field. LO-30's stated example, applied to a marking problem.
Three ways magnets lose magnetism and why storage matters. Practical care of equipment, LO-36.
Infer that Earth's pole near geographic North is magnetically South. Reasoning from an observed alignment back to its cause, LO-31.
Two magnet-carrying toy cars attracting and repelling, and what the facing poles must be. Applying the pole rule to a hidden arrangement, LO-32.

Scrap-lifting crane: part (ii) contrasts an electromagnet with a permanent magnet (LO-28), part (iii) evaluates which suits the job (LO-36). NEP content the 13-outcome frame does not anticipate, so no LO names electromagnets.
Needles forming a chain on a magnet, and whether it survives the magnet's removal. The chain is explained by induced temporary magnetism -- a phenomenon related to its cause, LO-31.
Finding direction in a windowless room with thread, stand and magnet. LO-30 for the free-suspension investigation and LO-36 because the purpose is to find directions in a real situation.
A shop's magnetic security tag, its deactivation, and what a personal magnet would do. Magnetism applied to an everyday technology, LO-36; the frame has no LO for magnetic tags.
